deep_dive.title: Confidence-guided spatial gene expression inference for reliability-aware prognostic analysis from histology
deep_dive.abstract: Inferring spatial gene expression from histology images offers a promising strategy for extending spatial molecular profiling to large-scale clinical tissue archives. However, existing approaches face two major challenges: limited generalizability of single-cell expression inference across datasets and platforms, and the lack of reliable estimates of prediction uncertainty, which compromise downstream biological and clinical analyses. Here, we present REGAIN, a framework for spatial gene expression inference at both single-cell and spot resolutions with prediction confidence. Across tissue sections, independent datasets and platforms, REGAIN improved spatial gene expression prediction and downstream analysis. Confidence-guided selection further enriched for cells with more accurately recovered expression profiles and improved cell-type annotation, while confidence-weighted clustering enhanced spatial-domain identification. Beyond assessing prediction quality, confidence mapping reveals greater heterogeneity in gene expression predictability across spatial domains than across broad cell types, with differences persisting within the same cell type and associated with tumor progression-related cell states and local microenvironmental context. Importantly, in 766 patients from the TCGA-BRCA cohort, confidence weighting enhanced the prognostic value of histology-inferred spatial molecular features, yielding stronger prognostic associations and identifying additional prognostic information beyond age and PAM50 molecular subtype. These confidence-weighted features also showed improved prognostic discrimination compared with clinical variables alone or combined with unweighted spatial molecular features. Together, REGAIN marks a shift in histology-based spatial gene expression inference from a focus on predictive accuracy toward a reliability-aware paradigm, demonstrating that prediction confidence provides biological insights into morphology-expression coupling and enhances the clinical informativeness of inferred spatial molecular features.

deep_dive.title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
deep_dive.abstract: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

deep_dive.title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling
deep_dive.abstract: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test.

deep_dive.title: Multi-omics causal deep learning reveals regulatory structure while interventions refine perturbation predictions
deep_dive.abstract: Inferring gene regulation from single-cell data is difficult because observational measurements cannot distinguish correlation from causation and access to perturbational data, especially with multiple modalities, remains limited. Here we present the Cross-Modal Causal Variational Autoencoder (CMC-VAE), which learns a network linking genes and proteins (gene-gene, protein-protein and gene-protein) in the latent space and maps each connection back onto measured features. Trained on 809,130 observational CITE-seq profiles, CMC-VAE recovers co-expression, transcription factor regulons and immune signalling programs, and learns a sparse cross-modal map enriched for transcript-protein cognate pairs. On three CRISPR screens used during development, it ranks knockout-responsive genes better than correlation and latent-VAE baselines. Fitted to a screen's unperturbed control cells, without perturbation labels, the model translates measured knockout RNA responses into protein responses better than a correlation map and cognate transcripts. The direction of gene-to-gene regulation, however, is not recovered from observational data. On the CITE-seq screens, fine-tuning only the latent network improves held-out response correlation, mainly by learning a response shared across knockouts. On larger Perturb-seq screens, with about 1,000 training perturbations, fine-tuning the latent network learns gene-specific effects that transfer to held-out genes, more so than a gene-level causal model fine-tuned on the same cells, and in simulation, such interventions also restore edge orientations that observational training leaves unresolved.

quick_skim.title: CellBench: task-dependent performance and generalization limits of single-cell foundation models
quick_skim.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for transcriptomic analysis, yet it remains unclear what biological information their embeddings preserve and when they outperform dataset-fitted methods. Here, we present CellBench, a unified benchmark of frozen scFM representations across tissues, species, and genetic perturbation screens. We find that different models capture distinct aspects of cellular biology, while classical baselines remain competitive across tasks. Human-pretrained representations transfer to supervised mouse analyses, but under a shared decoder they fail to improve genome-wide absolute error over predicting no change for unseen perturbation targets. Neither model size nor reported pretraining data volume reliably predicts performance. Excluding cohorts with sample or donor identifier matches to pretraining records substantially reduces annotation advantages without changing model rankings appreciably. Together, these findings show that the value of scFM representations depends on the biological task and the strength of the evidence supporting their performance.

quick_skim.title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
quick_skim.abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

quick_skim.title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
quick_skim.abstract: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.
